messages.author: ddfc17f7a6fa5f53
messages.subject: Jacobian correction for differences / ratios
parts:
Dear all,

I quite recently adopted Bayesian methods for my work in plant / soil ecology. As I did not study statistics or maths I am currently struggling with the question, if I really need a correction in my application or not and if so how to do it correctly.

A few words on my data structure: I have samples from a factorial field experiment and for each of them two measurements are necessary for both Carbon and Nitrogen content. The used method requires at least 3 technical replicates. That means I have 4 * 3 measured values (2 * 3 for C and 2 * 3 for N) for each sample. First of all I am interested in the difference between the C (y[i] in the model below) and N values, respectively. As the first and second value for both C and N don't stem from one measurement procedure but from two, the values are not paired (i.e. C_1,1 is not corresponding to C_2,1 more than to C_2,2 or _2,3).

Most people would just calculate the mean of the technical replicates and do something like a two-way ANOVA-like analysis. As I was curious and also as a kind of exercise I decided to see what the difference was, if I did the mean calculations for the tech. replicates within the model (mu_C1[i] and mu_C2[i] below) in order to incorporate that uncertainty into parameter estimation. My (amateurish?) approach was as follows:

//Model for the difference of first and second measurement of C (C1, C2)
//Model for N is equivalent

  parameters {
    real mu_C1[Ntotal]; //mean of 3 tech. replicates for first measurement
    real mu_C2[Ntotal]; //mean of 3 tech. replicates for second measurement
  }

  transformed parameters {
    ...
    real y[Ntotal];

    for(i in 1:Ntotal) {
      y[i] <- mu_C2[i] - mu_C1[i]; //differences of means
     }
    }

  model {
    mu_C1 ~ normal(...);
    mu_C2 ~ normal(...);

    for(i in 1:Ntotal) {
      y[i] ~ ...; // use y in the context of a linear model
     }
    }

Of course, the warning message on transformed parameters and Jacobian transforms popped up and created some confusion. As far as I understand the background, this is a linear transform, which makes a correction unnecessary. Am I right in this point?

Next, I need to do a very similar analysis on the ratio of the differences in C and N, i.e. I would have a y_C (difference in C measurements) and a y_N (difference in N measurements) and would like to do a linear model on the value of y_C / y_N. Here, my confusion is perfect, as I guess I need a correction here, although a Jacobian matrix in this case would be a 2x1 matrix that does not have a determinant.

I hope, you can give me some advice on how to perform an analysis like this in theory and also on the question, if this approach is exaggerated concerning the data structure (when compared to just calculating the tech. replicates mean).

Thank you all in advance and best regards,
Christoph

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Jacobian correction for differences / ratios
parts: On Thursday, November 26, 2015 at 8:55:31 AM UTC-5, Christoph wrote:
My (amateurish?) approach was as follows:

parameters {
    real mu_y1[Ntotal]; //mean of tech. replicates for first measurement
    real mu_y2[Ntotal]; //mean of tech. replicates for second measurement

}

  transformed parameters {
    ...
    real y[Ntotal];

    for(i in 1:Ntotal) {

y[i] <- mu_y2[i] - mu_y1[i]; //differences of means
     }
    }

  model {
    mu_y1 ~ normal(...);
    mu_y2 ~ normal(...);

for(i in 1:Ntotal) {
      y[i] ~ ...; // use y in the context of a linear model
     }
    }

Of course, the warning message on transformed parameters and Jacobian transforms popped up and created some confusion. As far as I understand the background, this is a linear transform, which makes a correction unnecessary. Am I right in this point?

You are correct that a difference is a linear mapping. If d = a - b, then you have a mapping from (a,b) to (a,d) where d = a - b whose Jacobian matrix is

 1 0
-1 1

and whose determinant is just 1 * 1 - 0 * (-1) = 1.

However, it does not make sense why you are doing sampling statements for both y[i] and its constituent terms mu_y1[i] and mu_y2[i]. That is not illegal in the Stan language but it is very rarely necessary and yields an incoherent set of posterior beliefs otherwise. I think you can just put priors on mu_y1[i] and mu_y2[i] and use their difference however you want without putting a prior on y[i].

Next, I need to do a very similar analysis on the ratio of the differences in C and N, i.e. I would have a y_C (difference in C measurements) and a y_N (difference in N measurements) and would like to do a linear model on the value of y_C / y_N. Here, my confusion is perfect, as I guess I need a correction here, although a Jacobian matrix in this case would be a 2x1 matrix that does not have a determinant.

It is basically the same as above (and quite possibly unnecessary). You have a mapping from (a,b) to (a,r) where r = a / b whose 2x2 Jacobian matrix is

  1       0
1 / b  -a / b^2

whose determinant is 1 * a - 0 / b = a. In that case, you would need to do increment_log_prob(-log(a) - 2 * log(b)).

Ben

It sounds from the description like your mu_y1 and mu_y2
are measurements, not parameters. Or maybe parameters estimated
from measurements?

It'd also make things easier to understand if you named
the variables in your description (C and N) the same thing
as in the model (mu_y1 and mu_y2?).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Jacobian correction for differences / ratios
parts:
Thank you both for your quick and constructive replies.

Following Bob's advice I edited my original post a bit. The mu_C1 and mu_C2 values are really parameters of measurements, i.e. the mean values of three technical replicates. As I mentioned before I wanted to include these calculations in the model in order to catch the measurement uncertainty in the posterior. The reason I included sampling statements for y[i] AND both mu_C1 and mu_C2 is that I want to do a linear model (analogous to 2way ANOVA) on the differences (y[i]). So i need, I think the second sampling statement for that purpose, am I right?

I guess there will be better ideas to achieve what i want to do.
